paragraphs.heading: What it promises
paragraphs.text: Chebyshev's inequality, also called the Bienaymé–Chebyshev inequality, is a rule from probability theory. It puts a ceiling on how likely a random variable is to land far from its mean, as long as its variance is finite. Distance is measured in units of the standard deviation σ, which is the square root of the variance. The chance of straying more than kσ from the mean is then at most 1/k², for any positive constant k.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is so useful
paragraphs.text: Its strength is its reach. It holds for every probability distribution whose mean and variance are defined. That generality lets it serve, for example, in proving the weak law of large numbers. In practice it plays a role like the 68–95–99.7 rule, but that rule works only for normal distributions. Chebyshev's version promises, for a broad range of distributions, that at least 75% of values sit within two standard deviations of the mean and at least 88.88% within three.

paragraphs.heading: Only large k says anything
paragraphs.text: The rule tells you something only when k is bigger than 1. If k is 1 or less, 1/k² is 1 or more, and since no probability exceeds 1, the statement is empty. Take k = √2: the chance of a value falling outside the interval (μ − √2σ, μ + √2σ) is no more than 1/2. Turned around, at least half the values lie inside that interval.

paragraphs.heading: A worked example
paragraphs.text: Picture choosing a journal article at random from a source whose articles average 1000 words, with a standard deviation of 200 words. Two standard deviations either side of the average gives a range of 600 to 1400 words. The chance of landing outside it is at most 1/k² = 1/4, so at least 75% of picks fall inside. If you also knew the word counts were normally distributed, you could say there is a 75% chance of 770 to 1230 words, an even tighter range.

paragraphs.heading: The price of generality
paragraphs.text: Because it needs nothing beyond a known finite mean and variance, the bound is usually poor next to what extra knowledge about the distribution would give. The standard proof shows where the slack comes from. It throws away everything about values closer than kσ to the mean, and for values farther out it uses a lower estimate of k²σ² that can be quite crude. Even so, the rule cannot be improved in general: for each positive constant k, some random variable makes the inequality an exact equality.

paragraphs.heading: Who found it
paragraphs.text: The rule is named after the Russian mathematician Pafnuty Chebyshev, but his friend and colleague Irénée-Jules Bienaymé stated it first. Bienaymé proved it in 1853, and Chebyshev proved a more general form in 1867. Chebyshev's student Andrey Markov gave another proof in his 1884 Ph.D. thesis. The naming can confuse: Markov's inequality, a close relative, is sometimes also called Chebyshev's inequality, and some authors call the two Chebyshev's first and second inequalities.
